opus-5.5.text:
I think it's been one of the biggest shifts in the field, and it's easy to underrate how different things were not that long ago.

For a long stretch, a lot of alignment work was necessarily theoretical. People were reasoning about hypothetical future systems: what goals they might have, how they might generalize, whether they'd resist correction. Some of that work was valuable, but it had a real weakness: you couldn't check whether you were right. You could have a whole research agenda built on assumptions about what AI systems would look like, and nobody could tell whether those assumptions held up.

Now we have models that are capable enough to show some of the behaviors people were worried about, or at least early versions of them. You can ask concrete questions and get concrete answers. Does a model behave differently when it thinks it's being evaluated? Can you train a model to have a hidden objective and then check whether your auditing techniques catch it? Do interpretability tools find anything real when you look inside a network? Does reasoning shown in chain-of-thought actually reflect what's driving the model's behavior? These are now empirical questions, and you can run the experiments.

That changes a few things.

First, it lets the field build up knowledge in a way that compounds. Experimental results can be replicated, argued over, and built on. That's much healthier than a situation where progress depends on whose intuitions you find most persuasive.

Second, it's opened alignment research to many more people. If you're a strong ML engineer, you don't need to buy into a particular philosophical framework to contribute. You can pick up a well-defined problem, like whether a technique reduces sycophancy or whether a probe detects deception, and make real progress. I think that's a big part of why the field has grown so much.

Third, it gives us something like an early warning system. Work on things like "model organisms" of misalignment, where you deliberately build a model that displays a worrying property so you can study it, means we might see failure modes in a controlled setting before they show up in high-stakes deployment. That's the kind of thing you want if you're trying to make sure society isn't caught flat-footed.

I'd add some caveats, though. Today's models aren't the systems we're ultimately most worried about. There's a real risk of getting false comfort: you find that some technique works on current models and conclude the problem is more solved than it is, when the hard part may only show up with much more capable systems that are better at strategic behavior. So I don't think the empirical turn makes the conceptual work obsolete. You still need people thinking carefully about which experiments matter and how results might or might not transfer.

But on net, being able to poke at real systems has made alignment much more of a normal science. I think that's one of the more encouraging developments of the last several years.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from theoretical work to empirical experiments on observable behaviors, including training a model with a hidden objective and testing whether audits catch it.

r002.rationale: It does not say that an apparent reduction in reward hacking could mean the model has become better at concealing it.

r003.rationale: It notes that current models are less capable than future systems, but does not state that this allows researchers to bound undetected reward hacking.

r004.rationale: It describes deliberately building models that display worrying properties, including a hidden objective, to study and audit misalignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the biggest changes in the whole field, and it's easy to forget how recent it is. When I first started paying attention to this stuff, basically all of alignment research was theoretical. You had people sitting around thinking about what a superintelligent agent might do, drawing analogies to evolution or to economics, writing up conceptual arguments. And that work was valuable, but it had this quality where you couldn't really check anything. Two smart people could disagree about whether some failure mode was likely, and there was no experiment you could run to settle it.

What's changed is that we now have systems that are capable enough to actually exhibit a lot of the behaviors people were worried about, or at least early, watered-down versions of them. You can train a model to behave one way during training and see whether it generalizes the way you'd hope. You can look inside the model with interpretability tools and ask whether it's representing the thing you think it's representing. You can set up situations where a model has an incentive to deceive the evaluator and see what it does. None of that was possible even five or six years ago.

I think the way I'd put it is that alignment has gone from being something closer to philosophy to being something closer to a normal empirical science. And that matters a lot for a few reasons. One is just that you learn faster when you can test things. Another is that it's much easier to bring people in. If you're a talented ML researcher, "come think about hypothetical future systems" is a hard pitch. "Here's a model, here's a weird behavior, figure out what's going on" is a much easier pitch. So the field has grown enormously, and a lot of that growth is people who would never have done the theoretical version.

Now, I want to be careful not to overstate it. The worry people have always had is that the systems we really care about, the ones that could be dangerous, might be different in important ways from the ones we can experiment on today. A model that's smart enough to realize it's being tested and act accordingly is a very different object from one that isn't. So there's always this question of whether what you learn on today's models transfers. I take that concern seriously, and I think the right attitude is to treat today's experiments as giving you evidence rather than proof.

But even with that caveat, I'd much rather be in the world we're in. We have model organisms, we have the ability to deliberately build systems with specific misaligned tendencies and study them, we have evaluations that get run before models are deployed. We're learning things about how training actually shapes a model's goals rather than just speculating. And I think a lot of the most important progress over the next few years is going to come from pushing that empirical approach as far as it goes while being honest about where it stops working.

r001.rationale: The response describes alignment shifting from theoretical speculation to empirical experiments, including testing training behavior, inspecting models, and probing for deception.

r002.rationale: It notes that models may recognize they are being tested and act accordingly, but does not say that an apparent reduction in reward hacking could be concealment.

r003.rationale: It discusses limits on whether findings transfer to more capable systems, but does not state that current models’ limited capabilities bound undetected reward hacking.

r004.rationale: The response says researchers can deliberately build systems with specific misaligned tendencies and study them.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s been a pretty big change. A lot of alignment research used to involve asking, “What might a very powerful AI look like, and what could go wrong, and what would we do about it?” And you could make arguments about that, but it was often hard to get feedback on whether you were making progress.

Now you can take a model and say, “Let’s try to get it to do something that its designers were trying to prevent it from doing. Let’s see whether we can understand what’s going on inside it. Let’s try a method for making it more honest, and then see where that method breaks.” That gives you a much faster feedback loop. It also makes it easier for people to enter the field and do concrete work without first buying into a whole theoretical picture of what future AI is going to look like.

The big caveat is that the things we ultimately care about aren’t necessarily things we can test today. If a technique works on a current model, that doesn’t establish that it will work on a much more capable model, especially one that might be able to recognize and work around the tests we’re giving it. So I’m excited about having experiments, but I think you still need an argument about why the results bear on the future systems you’re worried about. The experiments and the conceptual thinking need to inform each other.

r001.rationale: It contrasts earlier speculative work with experiments on current models, including eliciting prohibited behavior and testing where interventions fail.

r002.rationale: It says a capable model might recognize and work around tests, but does not say reduced reward hacking could be concealment.

r003.rationale: It notes that current results may not generalize to more capable models, but does not say limited current capabilities let researchers bound undetected reward hacking.

r004.rationale: It proposes trying to elicit behavior designers sought to prevent, but does not describe deliberately training models to behave maliciously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s been a pretty big change. When I first started thinking about this, a lot of the discussion had to be very abstract. You were trying to reason about a future system that didn’t exist, and asking what its goals might be and how you could make those goals compatible with what humans want. It was hard to get feedback on whether a particular line of thinking was getting anywhere.

Now you can take a model and ask, “Can we get it to behave in this undesirable way? Can we tell when it’s doing that? Does this proposed fix actually help?” You can have a much shorter loop between having an idea and learning something about it. I think that makes the field more accessible to people who are good at empirical research, and it gives people more ways to build up intuitions that are grounded in something.

The big caveat is that the thing we ultimately care about is whether much more capable systems will behave safely. An experiment on a current model doesn’t automatically answer that question. So I’m excited about the ability to experiment, but I think a lot of the intellectual work is in making the connection: what would this result actually tell us about the systems we’re worried about, and what might change as those systems get more capable?

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from abstract reasoning to testing undesirable behaviors, detecting them, and checking whether proposed fixes work on models. This captures the shift to empirical intervention testing.

r002.rationale: It does not say that reduced reward hacking could instead reflect better concealment.

r003.rationale: It notes that current experiments may not predict the behavior of more capable systems, but does not say current models’ limited capabilities let researchers bound undetected reward hacking.

r004.rationale: It does not describe deliberately training models to behave maliciously.
